paragraphs: When observations contain two ordered times, ordinary independence is already ruled out: the second event must follow the first. The useful question is whether there is additional dependence beyond that ordering. This paper develops a statistical test for this property, called quasi-independence, with examples including account creation and first purchase, or clinical recruitment and survival.

The proposed nonparametric test considers a potentially infinite collection of alternatives. It can therefore look for dependence without requiring researchers to specify its form beforehand. Familiar procedures, including conditional Kendall’s tau and log-rank tests, emerge as special cases. The method also accommodates right-censored observations, which matter when a study ends or a participant leaves before the event is observed.

The authors analyze the test statistic’s large-sample behavior and evaluate the method experimentally. In those experiments, it detects dependence more effectively than existing approaches while requiring less computation. The contribution is a broader testing framework that preserves the distinction between dependence forced by time ordering and additional relationships that may affect interpretation.
neurips-2020-a-kernel-test-for-quasi-ind.tldr: A nonparametric kernel test detects dependence between event times beyond their required ordering, including with right-censored data.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in episodes of a fixed length, with a finite number of states and actions. Its central question is how efficiently a model-free learner can improve through interaction. Performance is measured by regret: the accumulated shortfall from acting optimally while the agent is still learning.

The authors propose UCB-ADVANTAGE and prove a regret bound of order square root of H squared times S times A times T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T is the total number of interaction steps. This improves the earlier model-free result identified in the abstract and matches the best known model-based bounds and the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

The algorithm also has low local switching cost and applies to concurrent reinforcement learning. These additional results address how learning proceeds when policy changes matter or experience is gathered concurrently. Together, the guarantees establish that model-free learning can approach the fundamental regret limit in this finite-horizon setting.
neurips-2020-almost-optimal-model-free-r.tldr: UCB-ADVANTAGE brings model-free episodic reinforcement learning within logarithmic factors of the optimal regret bound.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to design faster optimization algorithms for unconstrained, strongly convex problems. Its starting point is to change the objective being optimized while preserving its minimizer. Because the location of the best solution remains the same, progress on the transformed problem can still serve the original optimization goal.

The shifted objective expresses the original function’s smoothness and strong convexity through an interpolation condition. The authors construct an algorithmic template that explicitly exploits this condition. From that template, they derive several accelerated methods for settings with different first-order oracles, meaning different forms of access to first-order information about the objective.

For every derived method, the authors establish a faster worst-case convergence rate than the corresponding existing method. They also report that the interpolation condition makes the analysis both simpler and tighter, and evaluate the methods on machine learning tasks. The main contribution is therefore a reusable design principle: restructuring an objective can expose useful mathematical properties without changing the solution being sought.
neurips-2020-boosting-first-order-method.tldr: Shifting an objective without changing its minimizer yields accelerated first-order methods with improved worst-case convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence is useful only when it corresponds reasonably well to how often its predictions are correct. This paper studies that correspondence, known as calibration, and asks whether changing the training loss can improve it. The goal is to obtain predictions that remain accurate and confident while making their confidence values more reliable.

The authors show that training with focal loss produces models that are already well calibrated compared with training using standard cross-entropy. Combining focal loss with temperature scaling further improves calibration while preserving accuracy. They also analyze factors behind miscalibration and use those insights to explain the observed effectiveness of focal loss.

To make the approach easier to use, the paper provides a principled procedure for automatically choosing the loss function’s hyperparameter. Experiments span computer vision and language datasets and multiple network architectures. The reported approach achieves leading calibration performance without reducing accuracy in almost all tested cases. That qualification matters: the evidence supports a broadly effective training choice, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every model.
neurips-2020-calibrating-deep-neural-net.tldr: Focal loss, especially with temperature scaling, improves confidence calibration while preserving accuracy in almost all reported experiments.

paragraphs: A monotonic model has a predictable response to selected inputs: changing one in a specified direction cannot make the output move in the opposite direction. Such behavior can help address interpretability, fairness, and generalization concerns. Existing approaches either build monotonicity into restrictive architectures or encourage it during training without providing a proof.

This paper proposes checking monotonicity of general piecewise-linear neural networks by solving a mixed integer linear programming problem. The certification step makes it possible to use flexible model structures and then verify the desired property. Training uses heuristic monotonicity regularization, whose strength can be increased gradually until the resulting network receives a certificate.

The approach separates encouraging monotonic behavior from proving that the trained model has it. It does not require manually designed restrictions on the weight space. The authors report more accurate approximation than prior work and empirical efficiency advantages across several datasets, including comparisons with Deep Lattice Networks. Its guarantee concerns certified monotonicity on selected features; the broader motivation is to make that property available in less restrictive networks.
neurips-2020-certified-monotonic-neural-.tldr: Mixed integer optimization certifies monotonicity in piecewise-linear neural networks trained with progressively stronger monotonicity regularization.

paragraphs: This paper improves time-series forecasting with models whose hidden dynamics can switch between different linear Gaussian regimes. Such models retain useful mathematical structure, but richer forecasting behavior calls for additional flexibility. The authors extend the relationship between the hidden state and regime switches while preserving the part of the model that remains tractable when conditioned on other variables.

Inference uses a Rao-Blackwellised particle filter, and learning uses a corresponding Monte Carlo objective. The objective takes advantage of conditional linearity by calculating relevant conditional expectations exactly. A specially structured proposal distribution supports the sampling procedure. An auxiliary-variable construction with a neural decoder adds nonlinear observation models and accommodates observations containing multiple variables.

The resulting design combines richer dynamics and observations with calculations that still exploit the original model’s structure. Evaluations cover established forecasting datasets and image sequences from simulated physical systems. The authors report better forecasting performance than other deep state-space approaches in these experiments, supporting the value of preserving tractable components while expanding the model’s expressive capabilities.
neurips-2020-deep-rao-blackwellised-part.tldr: A neural extension of switching dynamical models improves forecasting while retaining exact calculations for conditionally tractable components.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimation requires comparing possible two-dimensional movements between images. Learning how to score candidate matches has helped stereo matching, but directly extending that machinery to optical flow would require an expensive five-dimensional feature volume and dense four-dimensional convolutions. This paper develops a way to learn matching costs without building that feature volume.

The method evaluates each candidate displacement independently using the same matching network built from two-dimensional convolutions. These evaluations form a four-dimensional cost volume. Sharing the matching network across displacement hypotheses provides the displacement-invariant component of the approach while avoiding the computationally prohibitive direct extension described in the abstract.

A displacement-aware projection layer then adjusts the costs while considering relationships among candidate movements. This helps address ambiguity when multiple candidates appear plausible. A two-dimensional soft-argmin layer converts the adjusted costs into a flow estimate. The authors report leading accuracy across several datasets and better Sintel performance than all published optical flow methods in their comparison. The result connects a more manageable matching computation with strong reported estimation accuracy.
neurips-2020-displacement-invariant-matc.tldr: Scoring displacements independently with a shared network makes learned optical-flow matching costs computationally manageable and highly accurate in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Local conditional estimation asks what to predict when particular input variables take specified values. The paper targets nonparametric estimators, which avoid committing to a fixed parametric form. Many existing methods emphasize relatively homogeneous data, leaving them sensitive to adversarial corruption and potentially unreliable when only a small number of observations is available.

The proposed estimator chooses a local estimate by minimizing the worst conditional expected loss across a collection of possible data distributions. This collection is a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Considering the worst case within that set makes uncertainty about the distribution part of the estimation problem itself, rather than relying entirely on the observed distribution.

Although this optimization is generally intractable, the authors identify broadly applicable settings where convex optimization can solve it efficiently. They establish robustness to corrupted and heterogeneous data and report competitive experimental performance. The practical significance is the combination of a protective estimation objective with tractable computation under the stated settings; the abstract does not claim that every version of the general problem becomes easy.
neurips-2020-distributionally-robust-loc.tldr: A worst-case distributional objective produces robust local estimates and admits efficient convex solutions in broadly applicable settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies fairness through the representation that a learning system builds from its data. It uses demographic parity as the fairness criterion: probabilities of model decisions should be independent of sensitive information. The authors argue that learning across multiple tasks can make it easier to impose this requirement on a shared representation.

Their method introduces constraints based on MMD and Sinkhorn divergences to learn that representation jointly across tasks. These quantities provide ways to compare distributions, supplying mathematical tools for the fairness constraints. The shared representation is intended to support multiple prediction problems while meeting the selected demographic-parity objective.

The authors derive learning bounds supporting transfer of the learned representation to previously unseen tasks. They also evaluate the method on three real-world datasets and report a significant advantage over the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The contribution links fairness and transfer: knowledge shared across tasks can help shape a representation that remains useful beyond the tasks used to learn it. The fairness claim is specifically framed around demographic parity.
neurips-2020-exploiting-mmd-and-sinkhorn.tldr: Distribution-based constraints learn a shared representation that supports demographic parity and comes with transfer bounds for new tasks.

paragraphs: This large empirical study examines when finite neural networks behave like the kernel methods associated with infinitely wide networks. The relationship varies substantially with architecture and training choices. In the reported experiments, kernels outperform finite fully connected networks but trail finite convolutional networks, and neural-network Gaussian-process kernels frequently outperform neural tangent kernels.

Centering and ensembling finite networks reduce posterior variance and make their behavior closer to the infinite-network counterpart. Weight decay and large learning rates can break the correspondence. The study also finds advantages for NTK parameterization, similarities between kernel diagonal regularization and early stopping, and accuracy gains from regularized ZCA whitening. Numerical precision limits kernel performance beyond a critical dataset size.

Width does not produce a simple progression: finite-network performance changes nonmonotonically in ways double descent does not capture. CNN equivariance helps only narrow networks far from the kernel regime in these experiments. The findings motivate improved layer-specific weight decay and kernel prediction practices, including a new ensembling technique. With those practices, the authors report leading CIFAR-10 kernel results within each architecture class studied.
neurips-2020-finite-versus-infinite-neur.tldr: A large empirical study maps when finite networks resemble infinite-width kernels and uses the findings to improve both approaches.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often describes desirable behavior through rewards, but some requirements are better expressed as constraints on costs. This paper proposes FOCOPS, a method for improving reward while respecting such constraints. The setting is particularly relevant when an agent must learn useful behavior while avoiding actions represented as costly or unsafe.

FOCOPS divides each update into two steps using data collected by the current policy. First, it solves a constrained optimization problem directly in policy space without restricting the solution to the chosen parameterization. It then projects that update policy back into the parameterized policy family used by the agent. This separates the constrained policy decision from its representation.

The method uses first-order optimization, which the authors describe as simple to implement. They also provide an approximate upper bound on worst-case constraint violation during training. That result should be read as a bound on violations rather than an absolute claim that none occur. Experiments on constrained robotic locomotion tasks provide evidence of better performance for the proposed approach.
neurips-2020-first-order-constrained-opt.tldr: FOCOPS improves constrained reinforcement learning through a policy-space update followed by projection, with an approximate training-time violation bound.

paragraphs: This paper considers an agent controlling an unknown nonlinear dynamical system over repeated episodes. The dynamics are assumed to belong to a known reproducing kernel Hilbert space, although the particular function governing the system is unknown. That modeling framework accommodates discrete or continuous control inputs and can include dynamics that are neither smooth nor differentiable.

The authors introduce LC3, a lower-confidence-based control algorithm, and establish a near-optimal regret bound growing as the square root of the number of episodes. Regret measures accumulated performance loss relative to the optimal controller. The result describes how the cost of learning the unknown system grows as the agent gains experience.

A central feature is that the bound depends on information-theoretic quantities rather than explicitly on the dimension of the dynamics, which may be infinite. This makes the guarantee meaningful for the function-space formulation used in the paper. Experiments on nonlinear control tasks illustrate the algorithm’s application and demonstrate benefits from exploration when learning dynamics. The theoretical claim remains tied to the specified modeling framework and episodic setting.
neurips-2020-information-theoretic-regre.tldr: LC3 achieves near-optimal episodic regret for unknown nonlinear dynamics in a known kernel function space, using information-theoretic complexity.

paragraphs: Training one reinforcement-learning agent to handle several continuous-control tasks is difficult even when specialized agents can solve the tasks individually. This paper introduces KTM-DRL, a framework that transfers knowledge from task-specific teachers into one multitask agent. Its objective is to combine expert-level abilities across different tasks within a single learner.

Learning proceeds in two stages. An offline transfer algorithm first uses the teachers’ experience to quickly establish a control policy. That algorithm is designed specifically for an actor-critic architecture. The agent then continues learning online from newly collected transitions, with the teachers still providing guidance. This second stage lets it improve through fresh interaction after the initial transfer.

The authors evaluate the framework on two commonly used benchmarks from the MuJoCo continuous-control suite. They report evidence supporting both the knowledge-transfer and online-learning components, together with a large performance advantage over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The findings support teacher-guided transfer as an effective way to build a capable multitask controller in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-knowledge-transfer-in-multi.tldr: KTM-DRL combines offline teacher transfer with guided online learning to train one agent for multiple continuous-control tasks.

paragraphs: Dynamic speed scaling adjusts computing resources to reduce energy use as work arrives. The difficulty is that an online decision must be made before the future is fully known. This paper studies a version of the classic problem in which machine-learning predictions about the future can inform those decisions.

The proposed algorithm accepts predictions through a black-box interface. Its design therefore incorporates predictive information without tying the scheduling method to the internal workings of a particular predictor. The central objective is to benefit from useful forecasts while retaining a mathematical performance guarantee when those forecasts are very inaccurate.

The authors establish that sufficiently accurate predictions allow their method to outperform any online algorithm in the comparison described by the abstract. They also prove guarantees for the inaccurate-prediction case and provide experimental evidence supporting their claims. The advantage is conditional on prediction quality, while the fallback guarantee addresses poor forecasts. Together, these results show how future-oriented learning can be integrated into an online energy-management algorithm without making its guarantees depend entirely on accurate predictions.
neurips-2020-learning-augmented-energy-m.tldr: A prediction-assisted speed-scaling algorithm saves energy with accurate forecasts while retaining provable guarantees when forecasts are poor.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated learning of linear classifiers when the people or agents being classified strategically try to obtain favorable decisions. The deployed classifier can influence their behavior, so evaluating a learner requires attention to those responses. The authors use Stackelberg regret to measure performance in this strategic setting.

Their first result shows a strong conflict between Stackelberg regret and external regret. In worst-case scenarios, any sequence of decisions with sublinear external regret can have linear Stackelberg regret, and the reverse conflict can also occur. Thus, success according to one criterion need not translate into success according to the other when agents respond strategically.

The authors then design an algorithm that explicitly accounts for strategy and minimizes Stackelberg regret. They prove upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match, helping characterize the achievable performance for the problem. Simulations complement the theoretical analysis. The main implication is that learning against strategic behavior requires a performance criterion and algorithm that account for that behavior, rather than assuming ordinary regret control will automatically suffice.
neurips-2020-learning-strategy-aware-lin.tldr: Strategic classification can make standard and Stackelberg regret incompatible, motivating an algorithm with nearly matching Stackelberg regret bounds.

paragraphs: When several reinforcement-learning agents share an environment, independently pursuing their rewards does not by itself explain how cooperation will emerge. This paper gives each agent an additional ability: awarding rewards directly to other agents. The amounts are determined by a learned incentive function, making incentives part of the agent’s learning process.

Each agent learns its incentive function by considering how the rewards change recipients’ learning. It also accounts for how those resulting changes affect its own external objective. The mechanism therefore connects an incentive to its downstream behavioral consequences, rather than treating rewards given to others as having value independently of what those rewards accomplish.

Experiments in challenging general-sum Markov games show significant improvements over standard reinforcement-learning and opponent-shaping agents. The incentivizing agents often discover a near-optimal division of labor. These findings support learned incentives as a practical route to coordination in the evaluated environments. The broader prospect of promoting common welfare remains an opportunity and challenge identified by the authors, rather than a universal guarantee of the mechanism.
neurips-2020-learning-to-incentivize-oth.tldr: Agents learn to reward one another by anticipating how incentives change learning, improving coordination in tested multi-agent games.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning algorithm normally updates its policy or value function using a predefined objective. This paper instead lets an agent discover that learning objective through interaction with its environment. The objective is represented by a deep neural network, giving the agent flexibility in how it learns from experience.

The proposed algorithm uses meta-gradient descent to learn the objective while the agent is also learning its behavior. Because discovery happens online, the objective can change over time. The authors demonstrate that this process discovers ways to handle bootstrapping, changing conditions, and off-policy learning, all of which affect how experience should guide an update.

Experiments in the Atari Learning Environment show increasingly efficient learning as the objective adapts. Eventually, the method exceeds the median score of a strong actor-critic baseline. That finding concerns the reported median comparison, rather than superiority on every task. The paper’s contribution is evidence that an agent can improve its own learning procedure during interaction, using a learned objective that remains responsive to its ongoing experience.
neurips-2020-meta-gradient-reinforcement.tldr: An agent learns and adapts its own neural training objective online, eventually exceeding a strong actor-critic baseline’s median Atari score.

paragraphs: This paper brings ideas from sparse coding into deep networks for image restoration. Its focus is sparsity in hidden neurons: arranging the representation so that only some components are nonzero. The authors introduce structural sparsity constraints that work with gradient-based learning and can be attached to convolution layers in different networks.

The computational benefit comes from operating only on nonzero components. The paper reports that this can save computation without reducing accuracy. It also allows the representation to have more dimensions and greater model capacity with negligible additional computational cost. The distinction between available capacity and active computation is central to the proposed approach.

Experiments cover image super-resolution, denoising, and removal of compression artifacts. Across these restoration tasks, the authors find sparse neural representations to be important to performance. Their contribution is a way to incorporate sparsity into trainable network components while connecting it directly to computational savings. The results support the method as a means of expanding useful representations without paying the full computational cost of operating on every component.
neurips-2020-neural-sparse-representatio.tldr: Structured sparsity in hidden neurons reduces image-restoration computation and expands representation capacity with negligible added cost.

paragraphs: Recovering a rank-one signal matrix from noise often requires assumptions about the signal’s structure. Sparsity is one common assumption, but sparse principal component analysis has strong evidence of a gap between what data permit statistically and what computation can achieve efficiently. This paper studies a different assumption: the signal component lies in a generative network’s output range.

For an expansive Gaussian network prior, the authors analyze recovery with a finite amount of data. They establish an advantageous global optimization landscape for a nonlinear least-squares objective when the sample count is on the order of the generator’s input dimension. Their sample complexity is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The analysis covers both Wishart and Wigner spiked matrix models. It suggests that structured rank-one recovery with these generative priors may avoid a computational-to-statistical gap in the nonasymptotic regime. The specific network prior matters to the result: the paper provides guarantees under that structure, and presents the broader absence of a gap as a conclusion suggested by the analysis.
neurips-2020-nonasymptotic-guarantees-fo.tldr: Under an expansive Gaussian generative prior, rank-one matrix recovery has near-optimal sample complexity and a favorable optimization landscape.

paragraphs: Separately trained neural networks can often be connected by a curve through parameter space along which loss stays nearly constant. This phenomenon is called mode connectivity. The paper investigates a neglected complication: permutations of network weights create symmetries, so the arrangement of neurons can influence how easily a useful connecting curve is found.

The authors introduce neuron alignment, an inexpensive heuristic for approximating a suitable permutation. It encourages intermediate activation distributions along the curve to resemble those of the endpoint networks. They provide theoretical support for alignment’s benefit and use a proximal alternating minimization procedure to empirically verify local optimality of the selected permutation.

The experiments indicate that optimizing permutations is critical for efficiently finding simple, planar curves with low loss and good generalization. Alignment can also substantially reduce the robust-loss barrier between two adversarially robust networks, revealing models along the path with greater robustness and accuracy. The contribution is to make network symmetry an explicit part of connecting solutions, rather than leaving the curve search dependent on the original neuron ordering.
neurips-2020-optimizing-mode-connectivit.tldr: Aligning neurons before connecting trained networks helps find simple low-loss paths and can improve paths between adversarially robust models.

paragraphs: Multi-object matching seeks correspondences across a collection of objects. This paper proposes an efficient iterative approach designed to remain reliable when matching information is problematic. It begins by identifying serious limitations in existing approaches and explaining why the standard iteratively reweighted least-squares procedure is inappropriate for the problem.

The replacement is a new reweighting strategy that uses the graph connection Laplacian. Its distinguishing feature is that it incorporates information from higher-order neighborhoods. Thus, the information used to revise weights extends beyond the immediate neighborhood structure. This gives the iterative procedure a broader basis for judging the matching information it uses.

The authors provide partial theoretical guarantees and evaluate the procedure on both synthetic and real datasets. They report superior performance over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The combination of broader neighborhood information and a problem-specific reweighting rule is the main contribution. The theoretical support is explicitly partial, while the experimental results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in the tested settings; those are complementary forms of evidence for its robustness and efficiency.
neurips-2020-robust-multi-object-matchin.tldr: A graph-based reweighting method uses higher-order neighborhood information to improve robust multi-object matching in synthetic and real-data experiments.

paragraphs: Submodularity captures diminishing returns as a selection grows. For sequences, the order of selected elements also affects their value, making robust selection more complicated than choosing an unordered set. This paper studies how to choose a length-limited sequence that retains value when some selected elements are removed through failures or adversarial action.

The authors develop two greedy algorithms with different protection guarantees. One achieves a constant approximation ratio when the removed elements form a contiguous portion of the sequence. The other handles arbitrary removals, but requires a stronger assumption and has an approximation ratio that depends on how many elements are removed.

The analysis addresses differences among definitions of sequence submodularity and the separate roles of forward and backward monotonicity. These properties are consequential for proving performance guarantees rather than interchangeable technical choices. The authors also extend their analyses to approximate forms of submodularity and backward monotonicity. The results make the tradeoff explicit: protection against a broader pattern of failures comes with different assumptions and a different quality guarantee.
neurips-2020-robust-sequence-submodular-.tldr: Two greedy algorithms provide different guarantees for sequence selection that remains useful after contiguous or arbitrary element removals.

paragraphs: Supermasks in Superposition addresses sequential learning across thousands of tasks without catastrophic forgetting. It starts with a randomly initialized network whose weights remain fixed. For each task, the method finds a subnetwork, represented by a supermask, that performs well. Learning therefore selects task-specific portions of a shared fixed network.

When task identity is available at test time, the corresponding mask can be retrieved with minimal memory usage. Without that identity, the method searches for a linear combination of learned masks that minimizes output entropy. In practice, the authors find that one gradient step is often enough to identify the appropriate mask, even among 2,500 tasks.

The paper also demonstrates two promising extensions. Uncertainty can signal a new training distribution and prompt allocation of another mask, allowing training without task identities. Separately, a fixed-size Hopfield network can implicitly store the growing mask collection as attractors in a constant-sized reservoir. These extensions broaden the approach beyond explicit task lookup while retaining masks as the central representation of task-specific knowledge.
neurips-2020-supermasks-in-superposition.tldr: SupSup learns task-specific subnetworks inside a fixed random network and can often infer the needed mask with a single gradient step.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning with stochastic budget constraints and losses that can change arbitrarily between episodes. The learner sees the incurred loss and budget consumption only after an episode ends. Unlike the earlier approaches discussed in the abstract, the proposed method does not require advance knowledge of the transition model.

The upper-confidence primal-dual algorithm instead uses trajectories sampled from the system. Its analysis combines optimistic reinforcement learning with a new high-probability treatment of the Lagrange multiplier process used in handling constraints. This connects uncertainty about the environment with the need to manage both performance and resource consumption.

The authors bound both regret and constraint violation by an expression proportional to episode length times the number of states times the square root of the product of action count and T, up to logarithmic factors. Bounding both quantities shows that learning performance and constraint management can be analyzed together despite unknown transitions and adversarial losses. A cumulative violation bound does not amount to a claim that every episode satisfies every constraint.
neurips-2020-upper-confidence-primal-dua.tldr: An optimistic primal-dual learner bounds regret and constraint violations under changing losses without requiring a known transition model.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimization methods have been observed to outperform ordinary stochastic gradient descent on important tasks involving attention models. This paper investigates one possible reason: heavy-tailed noise in stochastic gradients. Such noise makes unusually large gradient fluctuations relevant to optimization behavior, potentially creating difficulties that ordinary SGD handles poorly.

The authors provide both empirical and theoretical evidence linking this noise to SGD’s weaker performance. They establish tight upper and lower convergence bounds for adaptive gradient methods under heavy-tailed noise. They also demonstrate that gradient clipping plays a key role in handling that noise, connecting a practical optimization technique to the theoretical explanation.

Building on the analysis, the paper introduces ACClip, an adaptive method that clips individual gradient coordinates. Experiments on BERT pretraining and finetuning demonstrate superior performance for this algorithm. The conclusion is appropriately specific: heavy-tailed noise is identified as one cause of the observed gap, rather than a complete explanation for every advantage of adaptive optimization. The work links that cause to both convergence guarantees and a concrete training method.
neurips-2020-why-are-adaptive-methods-go.tldr: Heavy-tailed gradient noise helps explain adaptive optimization’s advantage, motivating a coordinate-wise clipping method with strong reported BERT performance.
